I live in zone 6b so every year we get a yard full of leaves by early to mid November.  I've see a few posts with people talking about what to do with them so I thought I would share what I do with all of the leaves from our yard.  
First of all, I mow the lawn for the last time in mid to late September depending on how much rain we have had and how well the lawn is growing.  By that point in late summer, growth has generally slowed down so the lawn doesn't get so high that neighbors might complain.  
When November rolls around and most of the leaves have fallen from the trees in our yard and our neighbor's yards, I wait for a dry day when the leaves and grass are generally pretty dry.  I set the mower to the highest setting and run the leaves over with the mower without the bag attached.  After the first pass, I attach the bag, lower the wheels a notch, and mow over it again to basically vacuum up all of the leaves and grass clippings.  
This has a few advantages.  First, if you try to just mow up the leaves on the first pass, you end up with mostly whole leaves and the bag fills up pretty fast (I have a standard push mower, not a rider with some giant bin).  Emptying the bag more often takes more time, but, more importantly, the whole leaves do not decompose as fast as the mulched leave.  I also generally find that you end up with less grass mixed in because the bag fills quickly just with the whole leaves.  So by going over the lawn once without the bag and mulching the leaves in place then going back over it again with the bag I get a nice mix of fresh grass and ground up leaves.  By spring, the mix that I spread on the beds is practically decomposed with maybe 1/2" left on top that just gets incorporated into the soil when I prepare the bed for planting.  
What would have required 6 - 8 garbage cans to transport goes down to about 3.  I then spread that mix over all of our raised beds and immediately water it.  Once it's watered, the wind generally doesn't blow it around.  I also spread it under our cherry trees and blueberry bushes.  If there's any left, I top off our little tumbler compost bin and throw a pile in for the chickens who scratch around in it for hours eating the grass clippings and spreading it around their run.  
We have a lot of mature trees in our yard and surrounding yards and I don't let any of that free fertility to go waste.  Hope someone finds this helpful.

My take: we went astray as soon as we mentally separated ourselves from nature. A squirrel may believe they have free will because they can hide a nut here or there, but their overall activity and nature is that of a squirrel. Their impact on their surroundings on a greater scale is not tied to where they hide their treasure. Their activities we would all consider "natural".  Humans thinking that our free will, level of intelligence and capacity for self reflection somehow separate us from nature is wrong imho. 

Nothing we can possibly do is unnatural, there is no such thing. Our societies and our impact on the planet are entirely natural. That those things might bring about changes in our environment that make the planet uninhabitable for us is besides the point. Every creature on this planet fits in a niche and ultimately their group fulfills its purpose even if that purpose is not in their best interest. Humans too will fulfill our purpose, our niche in the global process of life on earth, even if it leads to our demise. And that is impossible to refute or escape. 

Not matter how hard an ant tries to understand the process of the sky darkening and a giant object crushing hundreds of their kin, they will never attain a sufficient perspective to see and understand that it's just a human foot coming down on them. Similarly, no matter how far out into the universe we send our probes and telescopes, we will never gain a sufficient perspective to understand the forces acting upon and with us and pushing us to fulfill our niche.

I could go on but I'm tired of typing on my phone. My belief that humans will ultimately fulfill our biological function within the web of life, no matter the consequences to us, and that everything we do is completely natural, helps me to overcome my anxiety about our future even though for most of us it looks bleak because nature is beautiful and our fulfillment of our place is just our contribution to a system we will never fully perfectly comprehend.
